title: Put the limiter at the door.
lede: A rate limiter is a design, not a middleware slogan (plate 33). Put it at the edge — gateway or a shared Redis — so every replica agrees on the budget. Token bucket: tokens refill at r/sec, burst ≤ bucket. Sliding window is fairer and more Redis ops.
diagram: Left (bad): limiter in each app box. 8 replicas × 100/s = 800/s. User retries hop instances. Right (hit): API gateway → Redis INCR key=user:42 window. Lua: if count>limit return 429 + Retry-After. Token bucket: tokens = min(burst, tokens + rate*dt). Caption: 429 is the contract (plate 34). Hot user is a hot Redis key.
what: One shared counter per subject (IP, user, API key) per window. Gateway so the app never sees the rejected traffic. Token bucket allows burst; fixed window is cheap and spikes at the boundary.
why: SDE-2: design rate limiter. They want where it lives, what the key is, atomic increment, and 429 vs drop. Local in-memory limiters lie under load-balanced replicas (plate 35).
trap: Per-process counters behind a load balancer. Fixed window of 100/min: 100 at 12:00.99 and 100 at 12:01.00. No Retry-After. Limiting only the login path and leaving signup open.

title: Chat is a log, not a row.
lede: 1:1 chat is an append-only log per conversation. Message id is a snowflake (plate 93). Recipients read from an offset. Do not UPDATE a messages row to ‘edit history.’ The live path is a socket (plate 216); the source of truth is the log.
diagram: 1 conversation_id → partition. append {id, from, to, body, ts}. 2 unread: last_read_id per user. 3 fetch: WHERE conv=? AND id>? ORDER BY id LIMIT 50. Caption: group chat is fan-out (plate 203). Presence is TTL (plate 222), not a message.
what: Write is append. Read is range by id. Pagination is the last id, not OFFSET (plate 32). Media is a blob url (plate 207), not bytes in the row.
why: WhatsApp / Messenger screen. They want: conversation as a stream, ordering, unread, and ‘edit’ as a new event, not a mutation of the past.
trap: One global messages table ordered by server now() — clocks skew, two messages swap. Polling every second as the product. Storing the whole history in the socket server’s RAM.

title: Fan-out on write, or on read.
lede: A post with N followers can be pushed into N inboxes at write time (fan-out on write) or pulled from the people you follow at read time (fan-out on read). Celebrities make write-fanout a thundering herd. Hybrid: push to normal followers, pull the famous.
diagram: Left: fan-out on write. tweet → worker → each follower’s timeline Redis list. Fast home timeline. Celebrity 80M fans = 80M writes. Right (hit): hybrid. push to <100k; celebs stay in their own store; home mix merges (plate 204). Caption: plate 205 notifications are the same fork.
what: Write-fanout precomputes the feed. Read-fanout computes it on request (fan-in from followees). Hybrid is the real answer at Twitter scale. Queue the fan-out; do not do it on the POST thread.
why: Twitter / Instagram design. The celebrity problem is the whole interview. Say hybrid in the first minute.
trap: Always fan-out on write. Doing 80M Redis LPUSH on the request. No backpressure on the worker. Treating ‘followers’ as a query at read without a cache.

title: The feed is a mix, not a query.
lede: Home feed is not SELECT * FROM posts WHERE author IN (friends) ORDER BY ts. That is a scatter-gather every scroll. Precomputed inbox (fan-out on write) or a k-way merge of friend streams plus ads plus celebs. The mix happens in a ranking service, then you cache the first page.
diagram: 1 sources: friends inbox, celeb pulls, ads, seen-ids. 2 merge by score/ts (heap of k heads, plate 161). 3 cache first 50 for user. Cursor = last (ts,id). Caption: ranking is a model; correctness is ‘don’t miss, don’t dup.’ Seen-set is a Redis bloom or id set (plate 123).
what: Feed = mix of streams + rank + cache + cursor. Pagination is the cursor, not OFFSET. Deletes/unfollows are invalidations, not instant global rewrites.
why: News-feed design. They watch whether you try one SQL IN-list. Say mix, cache, cursor.
trap: OFFSET pagination on a live feed (plate 32) — items shift, dups and holes. Recomputing the whole feed on every scroll. No seen-set so the same post loops.

title: Notify now, or notify later.
lede: A notification is an event you may not deliver in the request. Hot path: write the event, enqueue. Workers choose channel: in-app, APNs/FCM, email, SMS. Online + high priority = now. Offline or low priority = digest. The user is a budget (plate 201) or they disable you.
diagram: Three boxes: 1 Event log — like, comment, payment. 2 Fan-out worker — prefs, quiet hours, collapse ‘5 people liked’. 3 Channel — APNs token map, email, in-app inbox. Caption: collapse is not optional; 200 like events are one push. Tokens die; handle 410 Gone.
what: Producer does not talk to APNs. Preferences live next to the user. Idempotent send (plate 225) so retries don’t double-text. In-app inbox is a log like chat (plate 202).
why: Notification system design. They want: async, fan-out, collapse, channels, and ‘the producer is not the pusher.’
trap: SMTP from the API box. One push per like. No quiet hours. Storing only the push, no in-app history. Treating APNs success as ‘the user saw it.’

title: Typeahead is a trie at the edge.
lede: Autocomplete is prefix search under ~50ms. A trie (plate 62) or an n-gram index, cached at the edge (plate 36). You do not hit Postgres on every keystroke. Rank by popularity, personalize only after the prefix is narrowed. Debounce the client (plate 24).
diagram: Left (bad): SELECT name LIKE 'jo%' on every key. Right (hit): CDN / Redis prefix → top 10. Miss: trie or Elasticsearch completion. Off-peak job rebuilds hot prefixes. Caption: ‘jo’ is a tiny keyspace; cache it. Personalization is a rerank of 10, not a new index.
what: Prefix data structure + aggressive cache + debounce. Results are a short list, not a search page (plate 217). Invalidation: new famous name → refresh that prefix, not the world.
why: Typeahead / search-as-you-type. Latency is the product. They want trie or completion suggester, not LIKE.
trap: LIKE '%jo%' (leading wildcard — cannot use the index, plate 2). Hitting origin on every key. Returning 1000 hits. No debounce so 10 requests per word.

title: The API does not hold the file.
lede: Uploads do not stream through your API boxes. Mint a signed PUT URL to S3/GCS, client uploads to the blob store, you get a callback or poll, then store the object key. Download is a signed GET or a CDN. The API holds metadata, not bytes.
diagram: 1 POST /uploads → {putUrl, objectKey, expires}. 2 Client PUT to S3, Content-Type checked. 3 webhook / complete → DB row url=cdn/objectKey, size, hash. Caption: virus scan and thumbnail are workers on the object, not the request. Multipart for >100MB.
what: Metadata in the DB, bytes in object storage, hot reads on a CDN (plate 36). Auth is the signature, time-boxed. Never persist the signed URL as the public permalink — sign at read.
why: Dropbox / YouTube-upload / avatar design. They want: your RAM is not a disk. Direct-to-blob is the move.
trap: multipart/form-data through Node into /tmp. Storing files on the app instance. Eternal signed URLs. Trusting client-supplied Content-Length without a cap.

title: Video is chunks, not a file.
lede: A 4K movie is not GET /movie.mp4 from origin. Upload to blob (plate 207), transcode into renditions (360p…1080p), slice into 2–10s segments, publish a playlist (HLS/DASH). The player picks a bitrate; the CDN holds the hot segments. Origin is for the miss.
diagram: 1 upload → object store. 2 encoder workers: 360/720/1080 + audio. 3 packager: .ts segments + .m3u8. 4 CDN. Caption: seek is ‘start at segment N’, not a new file. DRM and captions are extra tracks. Thumbnails are a sprite sheet.
what: Adaptive bitrate + segments + CDN. Metadata (duration, titles) in the DB. The player is the load balancer across bitrates. Pre-warm popular titles.
why: YouTube / Netflix design. They want: transcode async, segments, CDN, not a single MP4.
trap: Progressive download of one giant file. Transcoding on the upload request. No 360p ladder so mobile dies. Origin without a CDN on the first frame of a premiere (stampede, plate 94).

title: A crawler is polite BFS.
lede: A crawler is BFS (plate 59) over URLs with extra laws: robots.txt, per-host rate limits, canonical URLs, and a frontier that does not explode. The queue is the URL frontier; the seen-set is a Bloom + store (plate 123). DNS and robots are cached per host.
diagram: Left (bad): recursive scrape, no delay, ignore robots, crawl querystrings as new pages. Right (hit): frontier (priority queue: sitemap, pagerank). Fetcher pool per host cap. Parse links → normalize → seen? enqueue. Caption: politeness = one in-flight per host, crawl-delay. Recrawl by change-rate, not daily-all.
what: Frontier + seen + fetcher + parser + store. Normalize: lowercase host, strip tracking params, pick canonical. Seed from sitemaps. Respect 429 and robots.
why: Web crawler / search-indexer design. Politeness is the interview, not the HTTP GET.
trap: DFS recursion (stack overflow, not breadth). No seen-set → infinite calendar links. Crawling ?session= as unique. One global QPS so you DDoS a small host. Ignoring robots.txt.

title: Nearby is a geo hash, not a scan.
lede: ‘Cars within 2 km’ is not SELECT * FROM drivers WHERE abs(lat-?) < … on a million rows. Geohash (or S2 / H3) turns a point into a prefix. Nearby = this cell plus neighbors. Live locations are a short TTL in Redis; the trip is the source of truth in the DB.
diagram: Left (bad): full scan + Haversine. Right (hit): geohash precision 6 ~ 1km. GET members of cell + 8 neighbors. Filter true distance. Driver heartbeat SET with EX 15s (plate 222). Caption: Uber matching is nearby + constraints (car type, ETA). Quadtree/geohash both work; say neighbors.
what: Spatial index + TTL presence. Heartbeat updates the cell; a trip locks the driver. Recalc ETA on a smaller set, not the world.
why: Uber / Yelp nearby. They want the index, the neighbor cells, and why lat/lon BETWEEN is not enough at scale.
trap: Bounding-box SQL on an unindexed float. One global geohash with no neighbors (miss the car 10m over the cell edge). Storing every ping forever as ‘location history’ on the hot path.

title: Reserve the seat. Then charge.
lede: Ticketing is two commits, not one. First, hold the seat with a TTL (10 min). Then take payment. Then confirm. If pay fails or TTL fires, the hold expires and the seat returns. Two users on seat A is a compare-and-swap or a version (plate 76), not hope.
diagram: 1 SELECT seat WHERE status=free. UPDATE … version=version+1 WHERE version=?. 2 status=held, expire_at=now+10m. 3 payment intent. 4 confirm → sold, or expire job → free. Caption: oversell is a lost UPDATE. Queue the flash sale (plate 94). Payment is a ledger (plate 215), not a boolean paid.
what: Hold ≠ sold. TTL + a worker that releases. Idempotent confirm (plate 225) so double-click doesn’t double-charge. Inventory is the scarce row; money is a different system.
why: Ticketmaster / booking. They want the hold, the race, and why you do not charge first (refunds are harder than a released hold).
trap: CHECK constraint only, no version. Charging before the hold. Holds that never expire. Flash sale hitting one row without a queue.

title: Name the eviction before the cache.
lede: A cache without an eviction story is a rumor you never expire (plate 8). Pick: TTL, LRU (plate 150), or write-through / write-behind. Then pick what happens on miss: one thread fills (lock / singleflight) so a stampede doesn’t melt the DB (plate 94).
diagram: Box1 TTL — news, sessions. Box2 LRU — hot keys, bounded RAM. Box3 miss — singleflight: first miss loads, waiters share. Caption: write-through: write DB and cache together. Write-behind: cache then async DB — faster, can lose writes. Aside: cache-aside is the default: app reads cache, on miss DB, then SET.
what: Policy first: what is stale, what is evicted, who fills. Key design: include the version so deploys don’t serve old schema. Null-cache the misses or they hammer 404s.
why: ‘Design a cache’ or any read-heavy system. Interviewers want stampede + eviction, not ‘we’ll add Redis.’
trap: Infinite TTL. Caching a user object without the id in the key (cross-user leak). No lock on miss. Write-behind as if it were durable.

title: One door. Many rooms.
lede: An API gateway is the load balancer that speaks product: auth, rate limit (plate 201), routing, TLS (plate 78), request ids. Apps behind it do not each reimplement JWT. A BFF (backend for frontend) is a per-client gateway: mobile wants different shapes than web.
diagram: Left: every service verifies JWT, CORS, limits — drift. Right (hit): Client → gateway (TLS, auth, 429, route /v1/users → users, /v1/pay → payments) → services. Caption: gateway is not the monolith. Timeouts and circuit breakers live here too (plates 19, 39). GraphQL can be a BFF.
what: Cross-cutting at the edge. Routing by path/host. AuthN here; authZ still in the service that owns the data (plate 14). One request id through logs (plate 84).
why: Microservices design. They want a door, not 40 copies of CORS. Contrast: the gateway does not own SQL.
trap: Putting business rules in the gateway until it is the monolith. Gateway as the only authZ. No timeout so a sick payment service holds every mobile request.

title: A leaderboard is a sorted set.
lede: Top 100 by score is not ORDER BY score DESC on every profile view. A sorted set (Redis ZSET, or a skip list / btree, plate 124) keeps score → member. ZADD is O(log n). ZREVRANGE 0 99 is the page. Rank of one user is ZREVRANK. Daily boards are a key per window.
diagram: Left (bad): SELECT … ORDER BY score LIMIT 100 every hit; ties scramble. Right (hit): ZADD lb:global 1840 ada. ZREVRANGE 0 99 WITHSCORES. Window: lb:2026-08-26. Caption: ties: score then userId as the second key so order is stable. Millions of users: shard by game, not one key of 1e8 (or use a pruned top-k).
what: Ordered index, not a sort at read. Time windows are extra keys. Writes update the set; the profile row can lag. Top-k only? You can drop members below the cutoff.
why: Game / sales leaderboard. They want O(log n) update + range, not a table scan.
trap: Sorting n users in the API. One giant ZSET of the whole company forever. Unstable ties. Recomputing the board with a cron every 5 minutes as the only design (fine for cold, not for live play).

title: Money is a ledger, not a field.
whisper: Double entry · balance is a sum
lede: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 is a race (plate 73) and an audit hole. A ledger is append-only entries: debit A, credit B, same tx, same amount. Balance is SUM(entries) or a snapshot plus tail. You can recompute. You cannot un-say a row — you reverse with a new one.
diagram: Left (bad): balance field, two writers, lost update, no history. Right (hit): tx 991: ada -10, store +10. Unique (idempotency_key). Snapshot balance nightly. Caption: money is integers (cents), not float. Currency is a column. Refund = opposite entries, not DELETE.
what: Append-only, double-entry, idempotent inserts (plate 225). Isolation is serializable or optimistic version on the snapshot (plates 40, 76). Outbox if you also notify (plate 224).
why: Payments / wallet. They want: never mutate money in place. Audit is the product.
trap: FLOAT dollars. Deleting a charge. Balance field as the only truth. Two-step ‘subtract then add’ without a transaction (plate 7). Using wall-clock as the unique id.

title: A socket needs a map of who is where.
lede: WebSockets at scale are not ‘open a socket to the API.’ Each connection lives on one box. User 42 may be on box C. To push, you need a map user → connection node, and a pub/sub (Redis, NATS) so any worker can publish and the owning box writes the frame. Sticky load balancing (plate 35) keeps the TCP.
diagram: 1 Client WS to edge (sticky). 2 Register 42 → nodeC in Redis. Heartbeat. 3 Chat worker PUBLISH user:42 msg. 4 nodeC’s subscriber writes the frame. Caption: 1M sockets = 1M fds. Horizontal: many nodes, one bus. Fallback: SSE or long-poll if WS is blocked.
what: Connection directory + pub/sub + sticky L4. Presence TTL (plate 222) is the directory’s expiry. Do not store the socket in Postgres. Fan-out to a room is pub/sub on room id, not a loop of 10k writes on one node if you can help it — shard rooms.
why: Chat / live comments / multiplayer. The map is the design. Without it you broadcast to every node or you cannot find the user.
trap: One Node process with all sockets. No sticky so the handshake lands on a box that doesn’t have the TCP. Polling the DB for ‘messages to push.’ Forgetting half-open connections — heartbeat or die.

title: Search is tokens pointing at docs.
lede: Full-text search is not LIKE '%red shoe%'. An inverted index maps token → posting list of doc ids. Analyze: lowercase, stem, drop stopwords. Query: intersect/union the lists, then rank (BM25, or a model). Typeahead is plate 206; this is documents.
diagram: Left (bad): LIKE across 50M rows. Right (hit): doc 9 ‘red running shoe’ → tokens red, run, shoe. postings shoe: 9, 17, 80. Query ‘red shoe’ = intersect, rank. Caption: Elasticsearch / Lucene is this. Updates are reindex, not UPDATE in place. Pagination is search_after, not OFFSET.
what: Analyze → invert → query → rank → page. The DB remains source of truth; the index is a derived view (lag is OK if you say it). Filters (category, price) are bitsets or doc values, not a second SQL.
why: Design search. They want inverted index + ranking, not Postgres ILIKE. Mention lag and reindex.
trap: LIKE '%term%'. Reindexing synchronously on every keystroke of a doc. OFFSET 10000 on a ranked list. Treating the search cluster as the system of record.

title: Comments are a tree, served as a page.
lede: Comments are a forest under a post: each node has parent_id. You do not SELECT the whole tree for a viral thread. Serve one page: top-level by score/ts, then a slice of replies. Nested path (materialized path / nested set) makes ‘all descendants’ cheap; adjacency list makes insert cheap. Pick for the query you actually run.
diagram: Left: adjacency parent_id, recursive CTE for 6 levels — fine for small. Right (hit): page of 20 roots + first 3 replies; ‘12 more’ is a cursor. Soft-delete hides a node but keeps children (‘[deleted]’). Caption: votes are a counter with a rate limit (plate 201). Realtime new comments: socket on post id (plate 216).
what: Tree in storage, page in the API. Cursors not OFFSET. Moderation is a state, not DELETE that orphans. Hot post: cache the first page.
why: Reddit / HN design. They want nesting + pagination + ‘deleted’ not CASCADE wipe.
trap: Loading 40k comments on first paint. Deep recursion in the API. Hard-delete that breaks the tree. Ranking every nested reply globally so a new child of an old thread never surfaces.

title: Labels explode the time series.
lede: A metric is a number with a small set of labels (plate 84). http_requests{code=200,route=/pay} is fine. http_requests{user_id=…} is a new time series per user — cardinality explosion, memory death, bills. High-cardinality truth belongs in logs or traces, not in Prometheus.
diagram: Left (hit): counters/histograms, bounded labels: code, route, method, region. Right (bad): user_id, email, request_id as labels — 10M series. Caption: histograms for latency, not an average you cannot undo. Exemplars link a spike to a trace id.
what: Metrics: cheap, aggregated, bounded label set. Logs: unbounded text. Traces: per-request path. Cardinality is the product constraint. Downsample old data.
why: Observability design. SDE-2s blow the metrics cluster in week one with a well-meant user_id label.
trap: user_id / URL-with-id as a label. Averages without histograms. One log line per metric scrape. Infinite retention at scrape resolution.

title: A flag is a remote if.
lede: A feature flag is an if you can change without deploying. Boolean for kill switches. Percent rollout hashed on user id (stable). Properties for ‘staff only.’ The client asks a config service (or a cached snapshot), not git. Flags die: a flag that lives a year is an unofficial config database.
diagram: 1 SDK reads snapshot every 30s (or push). 2 evaluate(flag, user) → hash(user+flag)%100 < 10. 3 default if the service is down — fail open or closed is a choice you say out loud. Caption: kill switch fail-closed for payments; fail-open for a new color. Expose who saw what for experiments.
what: Remote boolean / multivariate with a stable hash. Cache the snapshot so the flag service outage does not take the site (usually). Audit who flipped. Remove flags after full rollout.
why: Progressive delivery, experiments, incident kill switches. Design: where the if lives, and what happens when the flag service is down.
trap: if (user.id % 10) in five services with five different mods — not stable, not central. No default on outage. Flags that never get deleted. Using flags as the only permission system (plate 14).

title: A job is a message with a clock.
lede: Work you should not do on the request is a job: send email, transcode, expire holds. Put a message on a queue (plate 6). Delayed jobs have visible_at. Workers pull, process, ack. At-least-once (plate 92) means the handler is idempotent (plate 225). Retry with backoff (plate 19).
diagram: 1 API writes row + outbox (plate 224) or enqueue. 2 queue: SQS / Redis streams / Kafka. 3 worker: lease, do, ack. Fail → retry, then DLQ. Caption: cron is a special job with a schedule. Visibility timeout > work time or two workers grab the same message.
what: Async boundary + lease + ack + DLQ. Delay is not sleep() in the API. Ordering: one key → one partition if you need it; otherwise don’t pretend.
why: Almost every SDE-2 design has a worker. They want: why not in-request, retries, poison messages, idempotency.
trap: sleep(10 minutes) in a web worker. No DLQ so poison blocks the queue. Visibility timeout 30s on a 2-minute transcode — duplicate work. ‘Exactly once’ without an idempotency key.

title: Presence is a TTL, not a boolean.
lede: Online/offline is not a column you set on connect and clear on disconnect. Disconnects lie (laptop lid, killed tab, half-open TCP). Heartbeat: SET user:42:online EX 30. Miss three beats → offline. last_seen is the stamp you show. The socket map (plate 216) uses the same TTL.
diagram: Left (bad): is_online boolean, UPDATE on WS close — never fires. Right (hit): heartbeat every 10s, TTL 30s. Presence channel: pub ‘online’ on first SET, ‘offline’ on expire (keyspace notify or a scanner). Caption: ‘last seen 3m ago’ is better UX than a lying green dot. Mobile: longer TTL.
what: Expiry is the source of truth. Connect starts the TTL; heartbeat refreshes; expiry is offline. Don’t require a graceful close.
why: Chat, docs, games. Interviewers wait for you to distrust onclose.
trap: Boolean column. Trusting onclose. Heartbeat every 50ms × 1M users. Scanning the whole user table for last_seen < now-30s every second without an index / Redis.

title: The user has a home region.
lede: Multi-region is not ‘deploy the same compose file twice.’ Pin a user to a home region for writes (latency + data residency). Reads can be local replicas with lag (plate 99). Failover: promote a replica, or block writes until home returns. Cross-region writes need a story (CRDTs, or ‘home only’).
diagram: Left (bad): every write goes to all regions sync — latency of the farthest, or split brain. Right (hit): user.home=us-east. Writes to home. EU reads a replica. DNS / edge (plate 35, 36) routes. Caption: GDPR may force EU home. Session tokens include region. Failover runbook > magic.
what: Home for writes, replicas for reads, explicit failover. Global tables are a vendor feature with documented conflict rules — say them. Sticky sessions across regions are a trap; pin by user id.
why: SDE-2 multi-region. They want: who is the primary for this user, and what you give up (lag, or conflict).
trap: Active-active on a row without a conflict rule. Geo-DNS to a region that doesn’t have the user’s writes. Assuming replication is zero-lag. Storing region only in the client.

title: Write the outbox in the same commit.
lede: Dual write: UPDATE orders AND publish to Kafka in the app — one can succeed without the other. The transactional outbox: INSERT order and INSERT outbox_event in one DB transaction (plate 7). A poller (or CDC) publishes, then marks sent. At-least-once to the bus (plate 92); consumers are idempotent.
diagram: Left (bad): commit order; process crashes before publish — lost event. Or publish then crash before commit — phantom. Right (hit): BEGIN; insert order; insert outbox; COMMIT. Poller SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; publish; mark. Caption: Debezium CDC is the same idea without a table you own. Order of events is the commit order.
what: The database commit is the atomic boundary. The bus is downstream. Outbox rows are the durable queue. Delete or archive after ack.
why: The dual-write question. If you say ‘we’ll publish after commit,’ they will kill the process in the next sentence.
trap: Publish then commit. Commit then publish without an outbox. Poller without SKIP LOCKED so two publishers double-send (ok if idempotent, still messy). Giant outbox never cleaned.

title: Idempotency is a key you store.
lede: At-least-once (plate 92) and ‘user double-clicked Pay’ are the same bug. Idempotent means the side effect happens once (plate 29). The client sends Idempotency-Key. You persist key → response (or key → payment_id) uniquely. Retry with the same key returns the same result, not a second charge.
diagram: 1 header Idempotency-Key: uuid. 2 INSERT keys(k, user, hash_of_body) UNIQUE. Conflict: if body hash matches, return stored response; else 409. 3 do the work, store status+body. Caption: Stripe’s pattern. TTL 24h. GET is already idempotent; POST /charge is not, unless you make it so.
what: A uniqueness constraint is the lock. Same key + same body = replay. Same key + different body = error. The work must also be safe if two workers race — the unique insert is the mutex.
why: Payments, jobs, webhooks (plate 82). SDE-2 default answer to ‘exactly once.’ You cannot have exactly-once delivery; you can have exactly-once effects.
trap: Hashing only the URL, not the body. Keys without a unique index (TOCTOU). Reusing keys across users. No TTL so the table grows forever. Treating GET as if it needed a key.
